title: Graceful GPU shedding and traffic rebalancing for capacity-safe Dedicated upgrades
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Design and implement a coordinated, capacity-safe upgrade flow for Dedicated GPU pools that minimizes customer-facing outages during control-plane releases and node-level runtime upgrades. This ticket covers a new 'graceful-shed' orchestration mode that: (1) signals intent-to-drain with autoscaler-aware windows, (2) rebalances traffic away from draining nodes using weighted routing and request-level reroutes, (3) maintains a hot standby buffer to absorb bursty tail load, and (4) integrates rollout gates based on SLO regressions and error budget consumption. Goal: enable LTS-targeted patch rollouts with zero-customer-capacity loss for 95% of rolling events and clear, automated fallback for the remainder.
acceptance_criteria: Control plane exposes a drain-intent API that returns a lease token and expected drain window for a GPU node
Autoscaler honors drain-intent windows and does not terminate or scale-in nodes until drain token is released or expires
Routing layer can shift new sessions off draining nodes within 2s (configurable) and honor in-flight KV cache affinity for existing sessions
Canaries run for an LTS-targeted rollout with automatic pause on P99 latency increase > 10% or error rate increase > 0.2% over baseline
Rollout can be safely paused and rolled back within the same upgrade operation with automated capacity reallocation and no data loss for cached prefixes
End-to-end integration tests simulate autoscaler-triggered scale-in during upgrade without dropping requests in 95% of test runs
implementation_notes: Introduce 'drain-intent' metadata on node objects: {node_id, requested_by, lease_id, start_ts, soft_deadline, hard_deadline, min_spare_capacity}
Autoscaler change: when a node reports drain-intent, the scale controller treats that node as 'buffered' and will only scale-in after drain token release or hard_deadline
Routing change: add weighted routing rules that prefer non-draining nodes; for affinity we implement a 'kv-lease' header that allows a short-lived sticky period while migrating KV caches

Standby buffer: implement 'standby-pools' feature to pre-warm a fractional % of fleet (configurable by pool) to take on traffic while GPUs are draining; integrate with billing to ensure cost visibility
Rollout gates: implement a gate evaluator that reads short-window telemetry (5m p99, 1m error-rate) and computes delta against baseline; integrates with rollout orchestrator to pause/rollback
Operator CLI: 'rctl upgrades start --strategy graceful-shed --pool X --parallelism 10 --min-standby 0.05' to kick off an upgrade with parameters
Backwards compatibility: if older autoscaler doesn't support drain-intent, default to a conservative fallback mode that increases min-standby and uses lower parallelism
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (lab): run unit and integration tests with simulated autoscaler and routing in staging cluster
Phase 1 (canary): upgrade 3 small GPU pools (low-traffic customers) with 5% standby and gate-enabled monitoring
Phase 2 (regional ramp): increase to 20% of pools in the region, enable autoscaler-aware drains and routing shift; monitor for 48h
Phase 3 (fleet roll): run across remaining pools with conservative parallelism, auto-pause on gate triggers
Fallover: if gate fails in multiple pools, abort and start automated rollback using release tags and re-assign traffic to pre-upgrade nodes
test_plan: Unit tests for drain-intent API and lease expiry behavior
Integration tests: orchestrator + autoscaler + router in a local multi-node env simulating spikes and scale-in events
Chaos test: randomized node failures during an upgrade to validate fallback behavior
Performance test: ensure routing shift achieves <2s median time to redirect new sessions under load
E2E smoke in staging with real model workloads to verify KV cache migration and generation latency SLOs
risks: If standby buffer sizing is too small we may still hit tail latency spikes during correlated drains
KV cache migration could increase token utilization and cost if hot prefixes need to be repopulated frequently
Incorrect lease expiration handling could leak nodes into 'draining' state and block normal autoscaler operations
Complexity in routing may introduce a regression if not thoroughly tested with real traffic patterns
Rollout gate false positives could lead to prolonged roll pauses and increased operational overhead
